title: How do you verify Spark actually used a Broadcast Join (`df.explain("formatted")` → look for `BroadcastExchange` + `BroadcastHashJoin`), and what does the Spark UI show (no shuffle read/write on the broadcast side)?
shortTitle: How to verify Spark actually used a Broadcast Join

s1_definition.profdef: You verify a Broadcast Join by inspecting the query's physical plan and the Spark UI. Calling `df.explain("formatted")` prints the physical plan; a broadcast join appears as a `BroadcastExchange` node on the small side feeding a `BroadcastHashJoin` node, rather than an `Exchange` (shuffle) on both sides feeding a `SortMergeJoin`. In the Spark UI's SQL and Stages tabs, a confirmed broadcast join shows the large side with no shuffle read or write, a broadcast exchange with a small data size, and no sort-merge stages for that join.
s1_definition.analogy: Claiming the National Bank of India photocopied the small list for every clerk is one thing; proving it is another. You check the work order (the explain plan) and look for the instruction "photocopy and distribute the small list" next to "each clerk matches locally" — that is the broadcast exchange and broadcast hash join. Then you check the activity log (the Spark UI) and confirm the big pile of transactions was never carted across the room — no movement recorded on the large side. Both together prove the broadcast actually happened.
s1_definition.oneliner: Confirm a broadcast join by seeing BroadcastExchange plus BroadcastHashJoin in explain output and no shuffle on the large side in the Spark UI.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** You verify a Broadcast Join by inspecting the query's physical plan and the Spark UI. Calling `df.explain("formatted")` prints the physical plan; a broadcast join appears as a `BroadcastExchange` node on the small side feeding a `BroadcastHashJoin` node, rather than an `Exchange` (shuffle) on both sides feeding a `SortMergeJoin`. In the Spark UI's SQL and Stages tabs, a confirmed broadcast join shows the large side with no shuffle read or write, a broadcast exchange with a small data size, and no sort-merge stages for that join.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Claiming the National Bank of India photocopied the small list for every clerk is one thing; proving it is another. You check the work order (the explain plan) and look for the instruction "photocopy and distribute the small list" next to "each clerk matches locally" — that is the broadcast exchange and broadcast hash join. Then you check the activity log (the Spark UI) and confirm the big pile of transactions was never carted across the room — no movement recorded on the large side. Both together prove the broadcast actually happened.

**One line to remember:** Confirm a broadcast join by seeing BroadcastExchange plus BroadcastHashJoin in explain output and no shuffle on the large side in the Spark UI.

sections.s2_technical:
The first verification tool is the physical plan. You call explain with the formatted argument to get a readable plan, and you read it bottom-up because execution flows from the leaves to the root. For a broadcast join you look for two things. One is a `BroadcastExchange` node sitting on top of the small side's scan — this node collects the small side and broadcasts it. The other is a `BroadcastHashJoin` node that consumes the broadcast on one input and the large side's scan directly on the other. If instead you see two `Exchange hashpartitioning` nodes (shuffles) feeding a `SortMergeJoin`, then Spark did a sort-merge join, not a broadcast, and your broadcast did not take effect.

The formatted explain output also lists details per node, so you can confirm which side was broadcast and the join keys. You can additionally use explain with the cost mode to see the estimated sizes that drove the decision, which helps diagnose why a broadcast did or did not happen. If you used an explicit hint and still see a sort-merge join, the hint may have been ignored because the side was deemed too large, or the join type did not allow broadcasting that side.

The second verification tool is the Spark UI. On the SQL tab, clicking the query shows the same physical plan as a diagram, with a broadcast exchange node annotated with the data size broadcast — a healthy broadcast shows a small size there. On the Stages tab, the telling signal is that the large side has no shuffle read and no shuffle write for that join, because a broadcast join does not shuffle the large side. If you see large shuffle read and write numbers on both sides, that is a sort-merge join. The broadcast itself appears as a small broadcast task rather than a shuffle stage.

A senior-level nuance is reading the numbers, not just the node names. A broadcast exchange with a very large broadcast size is a warning sign that you broadcast something too big, which can cause driver or executor memory pressure even if it technically succeeded. Also, with Adaptive Query Execution enabled, the initial plan from explain may differ from what actually ran, because AQE can switch a sort-merge to a broadcast at runtime; in that case the final executed plan in the Spark UI SQL tab is the source of truth, and it may show an AQE-adjusted broadcast that the static explain did not. So for AQE queries you trust the UI's final plan over the pre-run explain.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — An engineer at the National Bank of India added a broadcast hint to a transactions-to-branches join but the job is still slow, so they suspect the broadcast did not happen. They need to verify from the plan. This is exactly what inspecting the explain output does — looking for BroadcastExchange and BroadcastHashJoin versus SortMergeJoin.

Problem 2 — Even with the right plan, they want to confirm at runtime that the large table was not shuffled. This is exactly what the Spark UI shows — no shuffle read or write on the large side and a small broadcast size.

The demo simulates parsing an explain plan string, detects whether it is a broadcast or sort-merge join, and simulates Spark UI shuffle metrics, logging a clear verified-or-not verdict with the evidence.

sections.s4e_build:
```bash
# Build
mvn clean package -DskipTests

# Run the demo
java -cp target/spark-join-verify-service-1.0.0.jar com.bank.spark.JoinVerifyDemo

# Verify in a real Spark job:
#   transactions.join(broadcast(branches), "branchId").explain("formatted")
#   # look for: BroadcastHashJoin ... BuildRight  AND  BroadcastExchange
#   # then open Spark UI → SQL tab (broadcast size small) and Stages tab (no shuffle on transactions)
```
sections.s5_journey:
Input data: two plan texts and two sets of shuffle metrics — one from a real broadcast join, one from a sort-merge join.

Step 1: For case one, the verifier scans the plan text and finds both BroadcastExchange and BroadcastHashJoin and no SortMergeJoin, so the plan evidence confirms a broadcast.

Step 2: It then checks the large side's shuffle metrics, which show zero shuffle read and zero shuffle write, so the UI evidence also confirms the large table was not shuffled.

Step 3: With both pieces of evidence agreeing, the verifier returns VERIFIED — the broadcast join is confirmed from both the plan and the runtime metrics.

Step 4: For case two, the plan contains SortMergeJoin and two shuffle exchanges, and the large side shows four gigabytes of shuffle read and write, so the verifier returns that it is not a broadcast join, which tells the engineer the hint did not take effect.

Step 5: The demo logs both verdicts and reminds that with Adaptive Query Execution the final Spark UI plan is the authority, since AQE can change the join at runtime.

Final output:

```
2026-10-30 04:47:00 [INFO] Case 1 (hinted join): VERIFIED broadcast join: plan + UI both confirm
2026-10-30 04:47:00 [WARNING] Case 2 (expected broadcast but got): NOT a broadcast join: plan shows SortMergeJoin or missing BroadcastExchange
2026-10-30 04:47:00 [INFO] Note: with AQE on, trust the Spark UI's FINAL plan over the static explain output.
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
I verify a broadcast join with two independent pieces of evidence: the physical plan and the Spark UI. For the plan, I call explain with the formatted argument and read it bottom-up. A real broadcast join shows a BroadcastExchange node sitting on the small side's scan, feeding a BroadcastHashJoin node that takes the large side's scan directly on its other input. If instead I see two shuffle exchanges feeding a SortMergeJoin, then Spark did a sort-merge, not a broadcast, and my hint or auto-broadcast did not take effect. The formatted output also tells me which side was built and the join keys, so I can confirm the correct side was broadcast.

For the runtime evidence I use the Spark UI. On the SQL tab the query diagram shows the broadcast exchange annotated with the broadcast data size, which should be small — a large size there is a warning that I broadcast something too big. On the Stages tab the decisive signal is that the large side has no shuffle read and no shuffle write for that join, because a broadcast join never shuffles the large table. If both sides show big shuffle numbers, that is a sort-merge join.

At the National Bank of India I used exactly this when a hinted transactions-to-branches join was still slow. The explain plan revealed a SortMergeJoin rather than a BroadcastHashJoin, which told me the hint had not applied, and once I corrected it the plan showed BroadcastExchange and BroadcastHashJoin and the Stages tab confirmed zero shuffle on the transactions side. The nuance I always add is that with Adaptive Query Execution enabled, the static explain output can differ from what actually ran, because AQE may switch a sort-merge to a broadcast at runtime, so for those queries the Spark UI's final executed plan is the authority rather than the pre-run explain.
